title: The autopsy
lede: Tap a cause to see the evidence. The percentages are our editorial weighting. The evidence under each one is sourced.

causes.title: A one-product boom
causes.text: The air-purification line was 40.0% of revenue in fiscal 2004 and 23.4% two years later. By our calculation about $181M of the $235M fall in revenue over those two years came from that one line.[^1] (derived)

causes.title: Credibility lost in court
causes.text: Consumer Reports panned the Ionic Breeze in 2002 and 2003. The company’s suit was struck in November 2004, it paid $525,000 of the publisher’s costs, and five class actions over the purifier’s performance followed.[^1][^4][^5][^16]

causes.title: Nothing to replace it
causes.text: Massage chairs, its other big line, fell from 9.1% to 6.3% of revenue. Average store transactions fell from $151 to $98 and sales per square foot from $618 to $383 between fiscal 2004 and 2006.[^1] An analyst told the Los Angeles Times the company had nothing new “that people overwhelmingly feel like they really need to own.”[^3]

causes.title: Turmoil at the top
causes.text: A shareholder fight in 2006, the founder’s exit in September, an interim chief executive and a stock-option review that restated three years of results all came as sales were falling.[^2][^3] Sales fell another 26% in the next fiscal year.[^6]

disclaimer: The weights are our judgment of how much each factor contributed. Reasonable readers could weigh them differently.
